title: Social Studies: Places and People
objectives: I can use ten words to talk about places on a map and the people who live there.
I can tell how people long ago settled near water and traded with others.
I can explain the difference between a region, a continent, and a landform.
I can write facts about a place using words from social studies.
rationale: Social studies reading in grade 3 assumes students can talk about where people live and why. The ten words cover three ideas: the map (continent, region, landform, harbor), the community (village, resident, population, capital), and what people do (settle, trade). Three of them (region, continent, landform) are Tier 3 geography terms taught beside the everyday Tier 2 words that make the passages readable. Capital is taught with its second meaning, a capital letter, because students meet both in the same week.

words.def: A large area of land that shares features, such as weather.
words.ex: The desert region gets very little rain.
words.ex2: Our region has cold winters and hot, humid summers.
words.nonExample: One small house on a street is not a region.

apps.academic: In social studies, we compare regions by their climate and landforms.
apps.spoken: Which region of the country do you live in?
apps.writing: Use region when you write about a big area with something in common.

cloze.s: The northern ___ of the state has cold winters, deep snow, and tall pine forests.

cloze2.s: Corn grows well in the Midwest, a farming ___ with flat land and rich soil.

misuse.s: The region was one small house on a quiet street with a red door.
misuse.why: A region is a large area of land, not one small house.

visual.alt: A map with a mountain area marked on it.

words.def: One of the seven huge areas of land on Earth.
words.ex: Africa is the second largest continent.
words.ex2: Penguins live on the cold continent of Antarctica.
words.nonExample: A single country or a lake is not a continent.

apps.academic: On a world map, we find the seven continents and the oceans between them.
apps.spoken: Which continent has the most people?
apps.writing: Use continent to name one of Earth's seven big land areas.

cloze.s: Asia is the largest ___, with more land than any other of the seven.

cloze2.s: Kangaroos are found on one ___, and it is also a single country.

misuse.s: Our school is the largest continent in the world, with seven oceans around it.
misuse.why: A continent is one of seven huge land areas, not a school.

visual.alt: A globe with a compass beside it.

words.frame: I would like to visit the continent of ___.

words.def: A natural shape on Earth's surface, such as a hill or valley.
words.ex: A mountain is a landform that rises high above the land around it.
words.ex2: The class built a clay model of each landform in the unit.
words.nonExample: A swimming pool dug by workers is not a landform.

apps.academic: In social studies, we name landforms such as plains, plateaus, and canyons.
apps.spoken: A canyon is my favorite landform.
apps.writing: Use landform when you describe the shape of the land in one place.

cloze.s: A plateau is a flat, raised ___ that stands high above the land around it.

cloze2.s: Wind and water over millions of years carved the canyon, a deep ___ in the desert.

misuse.s: A swimming pool built by workers is a natural landform that formed over millions of years.
misuse.why: A landform is a natural shape of the land; a pool is built by people.

words.def: A person who lives in a particular place.
words.ex: Every resident of the village came to the festival.
words.ex2: The residents of the apartment building planted a garden on the roof.
words.nonExample: A traveler who stays one afternoon is not a resident.

apps.academic: In social studies, we learn what residents of a town need, such as water and roads.
apps.spoken: I am a resident of this neighborhood.
apps.writing: Use resident to name a person who lives in a place.

cloze.s: The ___ of the small town voted to build a new library for everyone who lives there.

cloze2.s: A tourist visits for a week, but a ___ lives in the city all year long.

misuse.s: The visitor who stayed only one afternoon was a resident of the town.
misuse.why: A resident lives in a place; a visitor who stays one afternoon does not.

visual.alt: A person standing in front of neighborhood houses.

words.frame: A resident of my town can ___.

words.def: To give something and get something else in return.
words.ex: Early farmers would trade grain for tools.
words.ex2: Maya and Ken trade snacks at lunch.
words.nonExample: Keeping a sandwich and giving nothing is not trading.

apps.academic: In social studies, we learn how communities trade goods with each other.
apps.spoken: Do you want to trade cards with me?
apps.writing: Use trade when each person gives something and gets something.

cloze.s: Long ago, villagers would ___ wool for salt at the market.

cloze2.s: At recess, we ___ stickers so that each of us gets one we do not have yet.

misuse.s: Mia traded her sandwich by keeping it and giving Jon nothing at all.
misuse.why: To trade, each person gives something and gets something; Mia gave nothing.

words.def: To make a home in a new place and stay there.
words.ex: Many families settled near the river where the soil was rich.
words.ex2: After a long trip, the travelers decided to settle in the valley.
words.nonExample: Visiting a park for an hour is not settling there.

apps.academic: In social studies, we ask why people chose to settle near water.
apps.spoken: My cousins plan to settle in a new town.
apps.writing: Use settle when people make a home in a new place.

cloze.s: After sailing for months, the travelers chose to ___ near the coast and build houses.

cloze2.s: Birds will ___ in the bushes around the pond, build nests, and stay for the whole summer.

misuse.s: The explorers settled in the valley by leaving the next morning and never returning.
misuse.why: Settle means to make a home and stay; leaving the next day is the opposite.

visual.alt: A small house beside a river.

src.note: Settle also means to calm down; only the make-a-home sense is taught here.

words.def: A safe, sheltered place by the water where ships can stay.
words.ex: Fishing boats rested in the quiet harbor.
words.ex2: The town grew up around its busy harbor.
words.nonExample: A dry field far from the sea is not a harbor.

apps.academic: In social studies, harbors helped towns grow because ships could unload goods.
apps.spoken: We watched the boats come into the harbor.
apps.writing: Use harbor when you write about a safe place for boats.

cloze.s: During the storm, the sailors steered their ship into the calm, sheltered ___.

cloze2.s: Big ships unload their cargo at the ___ before trucks carry it to stores.

misuse.s: The big ships sat safely in the harbor in the middle of the dry desert.
misuse.why: A harbor is a sheltered place by water; a desert has none.

words.def: A very small town, often in the countryside.
words.ex: The village had one school, one store, and a small bakery.
words.ex2: My grandmother grew up in a mountain village.
words.nonExample: A huge city with tall towers is not a village.

apps.academic: In social studies, we compare life in a village with life in a city.
apps.spoken: Everyone in the village knows each other.
apps.writing: Use village for a small place where few people live.

cloze.s: In the quiet ___, everyone knew every neighbor, and the only store sat beside the well.

cloze2.s: The ___ was so small that the whole place could be crossed in five minutes on foot.

misuse.s: The village was a huge city with millions of people and hundreds of skyscrapers.
misuse.why: A village is very small; a city with millions of people is not.

visual.alt: Small houses beside a little church.

words.def: The number of people who live in a place.
words.ex: The population of the city doubled in twenty years.
words.ex2: A small island often has a small population.
words.nonExample: The height of a building is not a population.

apps.academic: In social studies, we use a graph to compare the population of two towns.
apps.spoken: The population of our town is about two thousand.
apps.writing: Use population when you tell how many people live in a place.

cloze.s: The ___ of our town is about two thousand people, so most families know each other.

cloze2.s: After the new factory opened, more families moved in, and the ___ grew each year.

misuse.s: The population of the town is how tall its tallest building is.
misuse.why: Population is a count of people, not a height.

visual.alt: A group of people next to a bar graph.

words.def: The city where a state or country's government meets.

senses.def: A big letter, like the A at the start of a name.
senses.example: Always begin a name with a capital.

words.ex: Washington, D.C. is the capital of the United States.
words.ex2: We visited our state capital and toured the government building.
words.nonExample: A tiny village with no leaders is not a capital.

apps.academic: In social studies, we find the capital of each state on a map.
apps.spoken: The capital is the city where the leaders work.
apps.writing: Use capital for the city where the government of a state or country meets.

cloze.s: The governor works in the state ___, where lawmakers meet to make rules for everyone.

cloze2.s: Paris is the ___ of France, and the country's leaders work there.

misuse.s: The capital is the town that has no government and no leaders at all.
misuse.why: A capital is where a government meets, so it must have leaders.

passage.title: Where People Settle
paras: Earth has seven continents, and each one has many regions. A region can be a desert, a rainforest, or a stretch of cold, windy coast. Every region has its own landforms, such as mountains, valleys, and plains.

Long ago, families began to settle near rivers and harbors. A harbor is a safe place for boats, so people who lived there could fish and trade. They traded fish for grain, cloth, and tools from faraway places.

Many of these places started as a small village. Over time, more residents arrived, and the population grew. Some villages became big cities. A few even became a capital, where leaders make laws for a whole state or country.

Today, you can still see signs of the past in an old harbor town. Narrow streets, wooden docks, and faded maps on the wall tell how its residents lived and worked. Each old building is a clue about what people needed and what they made.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "population" most nearly means
choices: the number of people who live in a place
qs.why: The paragraph says more residents arrived and the population grew, so it counts people.

qs.q: Why did people choose to settle near harbors and rivers?
choices: Water helped them fish and trade.
They wanted to avoid other people.
They could not find any land.
qs.why: The passage says a harbor is safe for boats, so people could fish and trade.

qs.q: Which sentence shows that a village can grow into something bigger?
choices: A harbor is a safe place for boats.
Faded maps hang on the wall.
qs.why: The sentence directly says villages became cities.

qs.q: What is this passage mostly about?
choices: How and why people settled places and how those places grew
qs.why: It explains where people settled, what they did there, and how communities grew.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten social studies words, read an informational passage about where people settled and how places grew, and use the words to describe their own region.

notes.va.region.n: Region is a large area with something in common. Ask students to name their region and one feature that makes it that way.
notes.va.continent.n: There are seven continents. Use a map and have students point to each. Do not confuse with country.
notes.va.landform.n: Landform is a natural shape of land. Students may call a building a landform; ask whether people built it or nature made it.
notes.va.resident.n: Resident means lives in the place; contrast with visitor or tourist. Link to reside and residence.
notes.va.trade.v: Trade means each side gives and gets. Compare with buy, where money is used, and with give, where nothing is returned.
notes.va.settle.v: Settle here means to make a home and stay. Students may know the meaning of calming down; note that this unit teaches only the home meaning.
notes.va.harbor.n: A harbor is a sheltered place for boats. Show a picture of a harbor and a picture of open sea and discuss why ships prefer the harbor.
notes.va.village.n: A village is very small. Ask students to compare it with a town and a city on a size scale.
notes.va.population.n: Population is a number of people. Use two local numbers on the board and ask which place has the larger population.
notes.va.capital.n: Capital has two meanings in third grade: a government city and a capital letter. Show both and ask which is meant in each sentence.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: "The passage says families began to settle near rivers and harbors. Settle means to make a home and stay. I think they chose water because boats help them fish and trade. I can point to that sentence as proof."
discuss: What would you need to settle in a new place?
Which is easier to find on a map: a region or a capital? Why?
misconceptions: Region is the same as country.
Population means all the buildings in a place.
Capital always means a capital letter.
Trade means to buy with money.
extend: Make a map of an imaginary region with three landforms and one harbor.
Find the population of your town and the capital of your state, then write two sentences using both facts.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit region, continent, and landform on a map two days later, again at one week, and use scarce, abundant, and drought when comparing places with different resources.
